newsitem.title: USA: Author who denied Japanese-Americans interned dies.
newsitem.headline: Author who denied Japanese-Americans interned dies.

text.p: A memorial service was held on Tuesday for Lillian Baker, a conservative author and lecturer who denied that Japanese-Americans were held against their will in Second World War internment camps. She died on Oct. 21 at the age of 75.

The Los Angeles Times quoted a spokesman for Baker's Americans for Historical Accuracy as saying she died at her home in Los Angeles. A spokeswoman for a nearby church confirmed a memorial service was held on Tuesday.

Baker, the widow of a Second World War veteran, had opposed recent reparations for interned Japanese-Americans and efforts to designate the Manzanar internment camp in California a national historic site.
She argued that Americans of Japanese heritage taken to camps after the Americans entered the war in 1941, were voluntary guests and free to leave as soon as they proved their loyalty.

"There were 25,000 people of Japanese descent who were residing in other states who were never touched. So how can we say this was racism?" Baker said in an interview with the Los Angeles Times in 1991.
She argued that far from being treated unfairly, Japanese-Americans benefitted from education and free food they received at the Manzanar camp.
In addition to founding Americans for Historical Accuracy, Baker wrote several books about the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbour and the Pacific theatre of the Second World War.
Her most recent book was "The Japanning of America: Redress and Reparations Demands by Japanese-Americans".
